---
title: "An introduction to spatial thinking and analysis using R as a crime mapping tool"
subtitle: "One-day hands-on workshop"
toc: false
---

This workshop introduces the concepts of spatial data analysis, using crime as our example. The aim is to get acquainted with how we represent place in data, the analytical decisions we make, and how these shape what we can say about crime, policing and criminal justice in the places they occur.

Research on crime and place is very good at telling us **what** happens **where**. It is less good at telling us **why** (Bannister et al., 2019). Keep that in mind today. Every map is built on decisions about representation, and those decisions shape interpretation.

We work through examples in R, using open data for **Leeds**. All code runs in your browser, so you can edit it and see what changes.

## How it works

- **Run Code** runs a block. Run blocks **top to bottom**.
- **Start Over** resets a block.
- Exercises have `______` blanks, a hint and a solution.
- First load downloads R into your browser (~1 min).
- Each part starts with a **Run me first** block that loads everything you need, so you can start any part fresh.

## Pick your route

- **New to R:** run the code, focus on the questions.
- **Know R:** skip Practical 0. Try the **Already know R?** boxes.

## Data

Study area: three wards of central Leeds: Little London & Woodhouse, Hunslet & Riverside, and Headingley & Hyde Park. We download most data live, from the same sources you would use in your own research.

- Crime, July and August 2026: [data.police.uk](https://data.police.uk/) API
- Ward and LSOA boundaries: [ONS Open Geography Portal](https://geoportal.statistics.gov.uk/). Contains OS data © Crown copyright and database right.
- Population, Census 2021: [nomis](https://www.nomisweb.co.uk/) API
- Streets: © [OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright) contributors (ODbL)
